title_jp: {颯太|そうた}の{作文|さくぶん}
context: Sunday at the farm. 田中さん's grandson 颯太 (11) is here from Nagano city for the weekend, and he shyly hands you his homework: an essay about the person he respects most. He wants your opinion before his teacher sees it.

phrases.jp: {私|わたし}の{意見|いけん|opinion|3}を{言|い}ってもいいですか。
phrases.en: May I say what I think?
phrases.note: A gentle way in before giving an opinion, at work or with someone older. Casual: {意見|いけん}、{言|い}ってもいい？

phrases.jp: {確かに|たしかに|true, certainly|4}、そうですね。でも…
phrases.note: The Japanese way to disagree: agree with part of it first, then add your でも. Going straight to 'no' sounds harsh.

phrases.jp: それはちょっと{違|ちが}うと{思|おも}うな。
phrases.en: I think that's not quite right.
phrases.note: ちょっと and 〜と{思|おも}う soften a disagreement; you'll rarely hear a flat {違|ちが}う！ except between close friends or kids.

phrases.jp: {漢字|かんじ}が{少|すこ}しずつ{読|よ}めるようになってきた。
phrases.en: I'm gradually getting able to read kanji.
phrases.note: 〜ようになってきた = has been slowly coming to (a change still in progress).

phrases.jp: おじいちゃん、{孫|まご|grandchild|2}にはほんとに{甘い|あまい|soft on, indulgent|3}ね。
phrases.en: Grandpa's really soft on his grandkid, isn't he?
phrases.note: {甘|あま}い = sweet, but also 'too soft, indulgent' with people: {子|こ}どもに{甘|あま}い{親|おや}.

dialogue_setting: 田中さん's living room, Sunday afternoon: 颯太's essay, written in pencil on squared essay paper.
text_title: {作文|さくぶん|school essay|2}「ぼくのおじいちゃん」　5{年|ねん}2{組|くみ}　{颯太|そうた}

dialogue.speaker: Opening
dialogue.jp: ぼくの{祖父|そふ|grandfather|2}は、{鷹ノ原町|たかのはらまち}でりんごを{育て|そだて|to grow, raise|3}ている。ぼくは、{家族|かぞく}の{中|なか}でおじいちゃんを{一番|いちばん}{尊敬|そんけい|respect|3}している。
dialogue.en: My grandfather grows apples in Takanohara. Of everyone in my family, I respect Grandpa the most.

dialogue.speaker: Every morning
dialogue.jp: おじいちゃんは{毎朝|まいあさ}5{時|じ}に{起|お}きて、{一本|いっぽん}{一本|いっぽん}の{木|き}を{心|こころ}を{込めて|こめて|to put into (feelings)|2}{世話|せわ|care, looking after|3}する。{口数|くちかず|how much someone talks|2}は{少|すく}ないけれど、ぼくは、それが{本当|ほんとう}のやさしさだと{思|おも}う。
dialogue.en: Grandpa gets up at 5 every morning and looks after every single tree with all his heart. He doesn't say much, but I think that is real kindness.

dialogue.speaker: Then and now
dialogue.jp: {小|ちい}さいころ、ぼくはりんごが{苦手|にがて|not keen on, bad with|4}だった。でも、おじいちゃんの{畑|はたけ|field, orchard|2}で{とれたて||freshly picked|2}を{食|た}べてから{大好|だいす}きになって、{今|いま}では{木|き}に{登って|のぼって|to climb|3}{自分|じぶん}でとれるようになった。
dialogue.en: When I was little I didn't like apples. But after eating one fresh from Grandpa's orchard I loved them, and now I can climb the trees and pick them myself.

dialogue.speaker: My opinion
dialogue.jp: {母|はは}は「おじいちゃんはもう{年|とし|old age|3}だから、{畑|はたけ|field, orchard|2}をやめたほうがいい」と{言|い}う。でも、ぼくの{意見|いけん|opinion|3}は{反対|はんたい|the opposite, against|3}だ。{畑|はたけ}にいるときのおじいちゃんが、{一番|いちばん}{元気|げんき}だからだ。
dialogue.en: My mum says, 'Grandpa is getting old, so he should give up the orchard.' But my opinion is the opposite. Grandpa is at his liveliest when he's in the orchard.

dialogue.speaker: This year
dialogue.jp: {今年|ことし}は、スペインから{来|き}たアルバートさんが{手伝|てつだ}ってくれている。おじいちゃんは{最近|さいきん}、{前|まえ}よりよく{笑|わら}うようになった。ぼくは、アルバートさんのおかげだと{思|おも}う。
dialogue.en: This year, アルバートさん from Spain is helping us. Lately Grandpa has started laughing more than before. I think it's thanks to アルバートさん.

dialogue.speaker: Ending
dialogue.jp: {将来|しょうらい|the future|3}はサッカー{選手|せんしゅ|(sports) player|3}になりたいけど、いつかおじいちゃんの{畑|はたけ}も{継ぎたい|つぎたい|to take over (a family business)|2}。おじいちゃんは、ぼくの{自慢|じまん|pride, something to boast about|3}だ。
dialogue.en: In the future I want to be a footballer, but one day I also want to take over Grandpa's orchard. Grandpa is my pride.

grammar.meaning: come to be able to / start doing
grammar.form: {可能形|かのうけい}: + ようになる ({読|よ}める → {読|よ}めるようになる, とれる → とれるようになる) · {辞書形|じしょけい}: + ようになる ({笑|わら}う → {笑|わら}うようになる) · no longer: ない → なくなる ({泣|な}かない → {泣|な}かなくなる)
grammar.explanation: Use it for a change that came with time: something you can now do (potential form + ようになる) or a new habit that has appeared (dictionary form + ようになる). It describes a result, not a choice: a resolution is 〜ようにする, a decision is 〜ことにする. With nouns and adjectives just use になる: {好|す}きになった, never 好きようになった.

examples.jp: {日本|にほん}に{来|き}てから、{納豆|なっとう|natto, fermented soybeans|3}が{食|た}べられるようになった。
examples.en: Since coming to Japan, I've become able to eat natto.

examples.jp: {最近|さいきん}、{父|ちち}は{毎日|まいにち}{散歩|さんぽ}するようになりました。
examples.en: Lately my father has started going for a walk every day.

quiz.question: {毎日|まいにち}{練習|れんしゅう}したので、{一人|ひとり}で{自転車|じてんしゃ}に＿＿ようになった。
quiz.en: I practised every day, so now I can ride a bike on my own.
quiz.explain: 'Became able to' = potential form in the dictionary shape ({乗|の}れる) + ようになる; the past goes on なる, not on the verb.

kanji.where: Printed on the pads of squared paper Japanese pupils write every essay on, one character per square.
kanji.related: {作文|さくぶん} = a school essay.
kanji.breakdown: {原稿用紙|げんこうようし}: 原稿 manuscript, draft + 用紙 paper for a purpose → 'paper for writing a draft on'.

tip.title: Whose grandpa is it?
tip.body: Speaking about your own family to outsiders, or in writing, you use the plain words: {祖父|そふ}, {母|はは}, {父|ちち}. For someone else's family you use おじいさん, お{母|かあ}さん. That's why 颯太's essay starts with ぼくの{祖父|そふ} and then slips into おじいちゃん, like every child does. Inside a family, people often name each other from the youngest child's point of view: 恵子さん may well call her husband おじいちゃん when 颯太 is around.

challenge.prompt: 颯太 looks up at you: 「ねえねえ、アルバートくんはどう{思|おも}う？おじいちゃん、{畑|はたけ|field, orchard|2}やめたほうがいいと{思|おも}う？」 Give your opinion (you agree with him), and say that you've become able to help a little. Use 〜ようになる.
challenge.hint: やめないほうがいい · {少|すこ}し{手伝|てつだ}える · 〜し
challenge.model_answer: ううん、やめないほうがいいと{思|おも}う。{僕|ぼく}も{少|すこ}し{手伝|てつだ}えるようになったし、{一緒|いっしょ}にがんばるよ！
challenge.explanation: やめないほうがいいと{思|おも}う gives your opinion softly (ない form + ほうがいい = it's better not to). {手伝|てつだ}えるようになった = potential form + ようになった, 'I've become able to help'. 〜し adds a reason, and plain casual speech fits talking to a kid.

vocab.note: Used in writing and about your own family to others. Spoken at home: おじいちゃん.
{尊敬|そんけい}する{人|ひと} = the person you look up to: a classic essay and interview question.
{心|こころ}を{込|こ}めて = with all your heart, wholeheartedly.
A softer way to say you dislike something: {納豆|なっとう}が{苦手|にがて}です.
{反対|はんたい}する = to oppose. The opposite: {賛成|さんせい} (agreeing).
{自慢|じまん}の{孫|まご} = a grandchild you're proud of. {自慢|じまん}する can also mean 'to show off'.

extras.title: My family, your family
extras.title_jp: {家族|かぞく}の{呼|よ}び{方|かた}
extras.intro: Left: your own family, when talking to outsiders or writing. Right: someone else's family.

items.jp: {両親|りょうしん|parents|3} → ご{両親|りょうしん}

items.note: Neighbours like ハナおばあちゃん will ask: お{孫|まご}さん、{来|き}てるの？

extras.title: Agreeing and disagreeing
extras.title_jp: {賛成|さんせい}・{反対|はんたい}
extras.intro: From warm agreement to soft disagreement.

items.jp: {賛成|さんせい|agreed, I'm for it|3}！

items.note: Slang, very common with young people.

items.en: I think it depends on the person.

items.jp: {私|わたし}はちょっと{反対|はんたい|against|3}かな。
items.en: I'm a bit against it, I guess.
